item.title: Top Executive Conference 2026 | Platform for leaders
item.description: The Fiji Commerce & Employers Federation (FCEF) is excited to bring you the Top Executive Conference (TOPEX) 2026 – Fiji’s premier business event – from November 19–21 at the Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa, Denarau. item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Commerce & Employers Federation (FCEF) is excited to bring you the Top Executive Conference (TOPEX) 2026 – Fiji’s premier business event – from November 19–21 at the Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa, Denarau.

Now in its 12th year, TOPEX continues to provide a national business platform where those who lead, influence, invest, regulate and build businesses come together to listen, share and contribute to the conversations shaping Fiji’s economic direction.

Reflecting on the role TOPEX has come to play, FCEF vice president and TOPEX committee chair Rowena Taito said: “TOPEX has become a cornerstone event for Fiji’s business community, recognised for bringing the right people into the room.”

“It provides a platform for business leaders of all sizes, investors, policymakers, decision-makers, development partners and industry voices to discuss the issues that matter to enterprise and contribute to conversations about Fiji’s economic future.”

Fiji continues to see potential across tourism, trade, investment, infrastructure, technology, green growth, MSME development, regional partnerships and new areas of enterprise.

However, these opportunities do not automatically become growth.

They require confidence, coordination, practical policy settings and a private sector that is ready to lead.

This is where TOPEX continues to play an important role.

The conference provides a space for honest, practical and constructive conversations — centred on the issues that sit close to every business owner’s reality – bottlenecks, policy, regulations, operating costs, investment opportunities, productivity, market access, partnerships and networks.

Some of the most valuable insights often come not only from formal presentations, but from the experiences shared by other business owners who face similar pressures, testing new ideas, entering new markets, managing teams, navigating regulation and finding ways to grow.

For large businesses, TOPEX offers the opportunity to understand emerging trends and connect with the wider private sector ecosystem.

For MSMEs and growing enterprises, it provides access to the thinking, networks and experiences of more established businesses.

For all delegates, it creates space to step back from day-to-day operations and think more strategically about the future.

Building on last year’s format, TOPEX 2026 will feature relevant, engaging and forward-looking conversations grounded in the interests and experiences of Fiji’s business community.

The team are carefully curating a programme that brings together business leaders, policymakers, technical experts and experienced practitioners who can share practical insights, introduce fresh perspectives and contribute meaningfully to the discussion.

As businesses respond to changing workforce needs, new technologies, emerging markets, regulatory developments and climate considerations, it is important to create opportunities to exchange experiences and consider what these changes could mean for enterprise.

The program is still taking shape and will be shared once it has been finalised.

Visit our website fcef.com.fj to get the latest.

TOPEX 2026 will once again be held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa, Denarau, from November 19 to 21, 2026.

This year, participant numbers have been limited to maintain the quality of engagement and the overall conference experience. Businesses and organisations interested in attending are strongly encouraged to register early.

Registrations for TOPEX 2026 are now open.

item.title: Sight can be saved — So why are we still going blind?
item.description: There’s a strange kind of tragedy buried inside the world’s eye health numbers. It isn’t that we lack the medicine. It’s that we have it, and still don’t get it to everyone who needs it. According to the World Health Organization, around 2.2 billion people around the globe are living with some form of vision loss. item.content:encoded:
There’s a strange kind of tragedy buried inside the world’s eye health numbers. It isn’t that we lack the medicine. It’s that we have it, and still don’t get it to everyone who needs it.

According to the World Health Organization, around 2.2 billion people around the globe are living with some form of vision loss. That’s more than a quarter of humanity. And here’s the part that should really stop you: nearly half of those cases — close to 1 billion people — didn’t have to happen. Their sight loss was either preventable in the first place, or is still treatable today, if someone reaches them in time.

So, what’s actually stealing people’s vision? Not exotic, cutting-edge diseases. Mostly ordinary, fixable stuff. Uncorrected refractive error — meaning someone simply needs glasses — and unoperated cataracts are, by a wide margin, the two biggest culprits worldwide. Glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration round out the list. A shocking amount of blindness on this planet traces back not to unsolved science, but to unsolved logistics: who can reach a clinic, who can afford a basic pair of glasses, who lives near a surgeon trained to remove a cataract.

And that gap isn’t evenly spread. It falls hardest on lower-income countries. Global eye-health surveys show that in low-income nations, about 80% of blindness comes from causes that could have been prevented or treated, compared with about 40% in wealthier countries. The same surveys found that vision impairment overall is estimated to be about four times more common in low- and middle-income regions than in high-income ones. This isn’t really a story about disease. It’s a story about distance — between people and the care that already exists.

You don’t have to look at the whole world to see this pattern. It’s playing out here at home, too.

A population survey of Fijian adults aged 40 and over found blindness affected about 2.6% of that group, with a further 7.2% living with low vision. Cataract was overwhelmingly the biggest driver — responsible for roughly 71% of bilateral blindness in the study — while among people with low vision, uncorrected refractive error accounted for about 63% of cases, with cataract behind another quarter. In other words: glasses and a routine operation, not rare or untreatable disease, sit behind most vision loss among older Fijians. (Source: International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB) Vision Atlas/ Fred Hollows Foundation)

Fiji’s cataract surgery story, then, is one of genuine, documented improvement — from a system that lagged its Pacific neighbours to one that now trains those neighbours’ surgeons and treats their patients. The harder work of ensuring the right patients actually reach that system, and reach it early enough to benefit, is where the next chapter has to be written.

Then there’s diabetes, which is reshaping Fiji’s eye health crisis in real time. The Pacific has some of the highest diabetes rates anywhere on Earth, and Fiji is no exception. Reporting from The Fiji Times, drawing on local research, found diabetes prevalence among Fijians aged 40 and over sits at around 41%, once adjusted for age, ethnicity and gender — with an estimated 60% of those cases going undiagnosed, especially in rural areas where testing is harder to reach. That matters enormously for eyesight, because diabetic retinopathy — damage to the blood vessels at the back of the eye — has become one of the leading causes of vision loss tied to the disease. Separate research across Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and the Cook Islands similarly identified diabetic retinopathy as a major contributor to visual impairment almost everywhere it looked, and found that not all of it was being treated with laser therapy even when it was caught.

The frustrating part is that the barrier often isn’t what you’d expect. A household survey in Fiji’s Central Division found that 86% of people knew of at least one place to get their eyes checked, yet only 66% of those who actually had an eye problem had ever gone. Older Fijians — precisely the group most at risk of cataract, glaucoma and diabetes-related vision loss — were the least likely of all to seek care. It isn’t only distance to a hospital or the cost of treatment that’s keeping people in the dark. Often, it’s simply not knowing help exists, or not believing it’s worth the trip.

Fiji hasn’t ignored the problem. Programs run with the Pacific Eye Institute and the Fred Hollows Foundation have trained hundreds of community health workers to screen for diabetic retinopathy and refer patients before damage becomes permanent, an approach designed specifically to reach rural and remote communities that clinics struggle to serve on their own. It’s a promising model. It just needs to reach a lot more villages.

Age plays a role in the global numbers too, but not always the one you’d expect. Diabetic retinopathy has become one of the leading causes of blindness among working-age adults worldwide — people losing their sight in the middle of their careers and their parenting years, often because a manageable chronic condition went unmonitored.

Children carry a cost as well. A global analysis from the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness estimated that uncorrected refractive errors among school-age children cost the world roughly 6.3 million equivalent school years and around $173 billion in lost economic productivity every year. A pair of glasses isn’t a small thing. For a child who can’t see the blackboard, it can be the difference between keeping up in school and quietly falling behind for reasons no one bothers to diagnose.

Here’s the part that ought to make health planners everywhere sit up: fixing this isn’t even expensive, as global health problems go. Research compiled by the same organisation found that eye care interventions return roughly $28 in economic benefit for every dollar spent — outperforming many other major health investments. Cataract surgery is one of the most cost-effective procedures in all of medicine. Glasses are cheap to produce and distribute. This isn’t a case of waiting on a scientific breakthrough. It’s a case of waiting on distribution, funding, and the political will to prioritise it.

Meanwhile, the numbers are still growing in raw terms, even as rates improve. Aging populations and the rising tide of diabetes mean the pool of people at risk keeps expanding, and some projections suggest the number of people blind from cataracts alone could climb by more than a third by 2040.

So why are we still going blind, in a world — and a country — that already knows how to stop most of it? Mostly because prevention isn’t glamorous. It doesn’t make headlines the way a new treatment does. It looks like training more community health workers, subsidising basic glasses, screening diabetics before damage sets in, and getting surgical teams into rural clinics and outer islands instead of only the main hospitals. It’s unglamorous work. But for a grandmother in a rural village with a cataract a twenty-minute operation could fix, it’s the only thing standing between her and a world going dark for no good reason.

Bikash Gyawali is a consultant optometrist & public health expertise at Asgar Eye Clinic

item.title: FIJI GETAWAYS | Where happiness finds you
item.description: STAYING at a resort offers travellers a complete holiday experience, combining comfort, convenience and relaxation in one destination. Unlike traditional accommodation, resorts provide a wide range of amenities and activities designed to suit different interests while offering the perfect opportunity to take a much-needed break from the demands of everyday life.
item.content:encoded:
STAYING at a resort offers travellers a complete holiday experience, combining comfort, convenience and relaxation in one destination.

Unlike traditional accommodation, resorts provide a wide range of amenities and activities designed to suit different interests while offering the perfect opportunity to take a much-needed break from the demands of everyday life.

One of the greatest benefits of staying at a resort is the chance to relax and recharge. Regular breaks from work are important for maintaining mental clarity, reducing stress and preventing burnout.

A resort getaway allows guests to step away from daily pressures and return feeling refreshed, energised and more productive.

Resorts are known for their luxurious facilities, including swimming pools, fitness centres and spa services.

These amenities encourage guests to unwind while also supporting physical wellbeing.

Activities such as swimming, walking and light exercise can improve circulation, reduce muscle tension and promote better overall health.

Many resorts are located in stunning settings, whether along pristine beaches, in the mountains or surrounded by lush tropical landscapes.

These peaceful environments provide the ideal backdrop for rest and relaxation while helping guests reconnect with nature.

Another key advantage is the exceptional customer service and variety of dining options available.

From local delicacies to international cuisine, guests can enjoy a diverse culinary experience without leaving the property.

Resorts also offer entertainment and recreational activities suitable for all ages.

When choosing a resort, travellers should consider factors such as budget, location, amenities and guest reviews.

With the right choice, a resort stay can provide the perfect balance of relaxation, wellbeing and unforgettable holiday memories.

Sigatoka River Safari, thrills and cultural spills.

Experience one of Fiji’s most highly internationally awarded day adventures with Sigatoka River Safari.

This unforgettable safari combines an authentic Fijian cultural experience with an exhilarating ride along the Sigatoka River aboard their tailor-made jet boats.

Your day will be filled with exciting 360-degree jet boat spins while making new friends and learning about everyday life in a traditional Fijian village.

Take a walk on the wild side and enjoy a taste of kava, Fiji’s ceremonial drink, during your village welcome and introduction.

Don’t forget to bring a towel you’re sure to catch a refreshing splash along the way!

Wild Adventures at Kula WILD Adventure Park

Located along the stunning Coral Coast, Kula WILD Adventure Park is Fiji’s only wildlife conservation park, offering endless activities for visitors of all ages.

Whether you’re eager to pet an iguana or in the mood for an exciting water slide adventure, there’s something for everyone to enjoy.

Kula WILD Adventure Park is proud to be Fiji’s only captive breeding facility for endangered indigenous species, caring for everything from turtles and colourful parrots to Fiji’s famous iguanas.

Make your family holiday both fun and enriching by discovering and learning about Fiji’s unique wildlife.

item.title: POINT OF ORIGIN I Fiji’s traders of change
item.description: LAST month, we looked into the Meridian Store and how a man travelled all the way from Navsari in India to start up a business on Taveuni. As Fiji developed, other Indians arrived not as labourers but as traders, craftsmen and businesspeople searching for opportunities.
item.content:encoded:
LAST month, we looked into the Meridian Store and how a man travelled all the way from Navsari in India to start up a business on Taveuni.

As Fiji developed, other Indians arrived not as labourers but as traders, craftsmen and businesspeople searching for opportunities.

Today, we bring to you the story of the first Gujaratis who came to Fiji.

While the arrival of the Leonidas in 1879 marked the beginning of the indentured labour system in Fiji, not every Indian who came to these shores arrived under that system.

Many came voluntarily, bringing with them skills, ambition and the determination to build better lives through trade and enterprise.

Among them were Gujaratis and Punjabis, communities that would become closely associated with business and entrepreneurship across the country.

From small village shops to larger commercial enterprises, these migrants helped shape Fiji’s economy while building lasting relationships with the communities they served.

Nearly a century later, their contributions remain visible in businesses that continue to operate across Fiji, including the well-known Meridian Store in Wairiki, Taveuni.

For Meridian Store managing director Champak Lal Dayaram, the story of these early migrants is one of courage, sacrifice and perseverance.

“Those people who came here had nothing guaranteed. They came to an unknown place, but they had the confidence and determination to build something,” he said.

“They started small. They worked hard, they understood the needs of the community, and they slowly established themselves.”

The arrival of Gujarati businesspeople in Fiji formed part of a wider migration movement that brought skilled workers and traders to the colony during the early 20th century.

Unlike indentured labourers who were recruited to work on sugar plantations, these migrants paid their own way or were sponsored by relatives and associates already living overseas.

Many left western India hoping to improve their lives through commerce, taking advantage of opportunities in emerging colonial economies.

Historical records show the first Gujaratis in Fiji were two goldsmiths from the Sonar caste who arrived in 1904 from Natal, South Africa.

Originally from Porbandar in the Kathiawar district of Gujarat, they travelled to Fiji with the assistance of Totaram Sanadhya.

Their arrival marked the beginning of organised Gujarati migration to Fiji.

Four years later, more goldsmiths followed.

Soon afterwards came tailors, barbers, launderers, shoemakers and other skilled workers from Surat and Navsari, bringing trades that were in demand as Fiji’s towns and settlements expanded.

Between 1916 and 1920, of the 752 Gujaratis who applied to migrate to Fiji, 336 came from Surat, 296 from Navsari and 120 from Kathiawar.

Patels also began arriving in 1914, mainly from Baroda State and the Nadiad district of the Bombay Presidency.

Although many had farming backgrounds in India, they quickly adapted to Fiji’s changing economy, opening grocery stores, drapery shops and laundry businesses.

Mr Dayaram said the willingness of these migrants to adapt became one of the reasons for their success.

“When they came here, they had to learn about Fiji. They had to understand the people, the culture and the needs of the community.

“They were not only thinking about themselves. Their businesses became places where people could access goods and services.”

In many rural settlements, small family-owned shops became more than businesses.

They stocked groceries, hardware, clothing and household necessities, often extending credit to families during difficult times.

For isolated communities, they became gathering places where news was exchanged and friendships developed.

Many shop owners knew their customers personally and understood the challenges they faced.

Mr Dayaram believes trust was the foundation that allowed many of these businesses to survive for generations.

item.title: MOTORING I Keep safe wear your seat belt
item.description: WEARING a seat belt is one of the simplest and most effective ways to protect yourself while traveling in a vehicle. Whether you are driving or riding as a passenger, buckling up significantly reduces the risk of serious injury or death in the event of a crash.
item.content:encoded:
WEARING a seat belt is one of the simplest and most effective ways to protect yourself while traveling in a vehicle.

Whether you are driving or riding as a passenger, buckling up significantly reduces the risk of serious injury or death in the event of a crash.

Seat belts are designed to keep occupants securely inside the vehicle, preventing ejection, which is often fatal.

One important fact to remember is that seat belts and air bags work together. Air bags are not meant to replace seat belts.

Instead, they provide additional protection during a collision.

Without a seat belt, a person can be thrown into a rapidly deploying air bag with tremendous force, increasing the risk of severe injuries.

To wear a seat belt correctly, always position the shoulder belt across the middle of your chest and away from your neck.

The lap belt should fit snugly across your hips and pelvis, not across your stomach.

Never place the shoulder belt behind your back or under your arm, as this reduces its effectiveness and increases the risk of injury during a crash.

A properly fitting seat belt is essential for maximum protection. When purchasing a new vehicle, check that the seat belts fit comfortably and securely.

If necessary, ask the dealer about seat belt adjusters or extenders.

Drivers of older vehicles equipped only with lap belts should contact the vehicle manufacturer to learn about upgrading to safer lap-and-shoulder belt systems.

Seat belt safety is especially important for pregnant women. Medical experts strongly recommend wearing a seat belt throughout every stage of pregnancy.

Proper seat belt use protects both the mother and the unborn baby in the event of a collision.

The shoulder belt should rest across the chest, between the breasts, and away from the neck, while the lap belt should be placed below the belly, fitting snugly across the hips and pelvic bone.

Pregnant women should never place the shoulder belt under the arm or behind the back, and the lap belt should never be worn over or on top of the belly.

Children also require special attention when using seat belts.

They should remain in an appropriate child safety seat or booster seat until an adult seat belt fits correctly across the chest and hips.

Buckling up every time you travel is a simple habit that saves lives.

By wearing your seat belt properly and ensuring it fits correctly, you can greatly reduce the risk of injury and help protect everyone in the vehicle.

item.title: MOTORING I A highland driver’s journey of dedication
item.description: WHILE most of Fiji is still asleep, 50-year-old Watisoni Kaitaci is already preparing for another long day on the road. Long before the first rays of sunlight appear over the hills of Wainimala, Naitasiri he has started his vehicle and begun the journey that has become part of his life for the past 15 years.
item.content:encoded:
WHILE most of Fiji is still asleep, 50-year-old Watisoni Kaitaci is already preparing for another long day on the road.

Long before the first rays of sunlight appear over the hills of Wainimala, Naitasiri he has started his vehicle and begun the journey that has become part of his life for the past 15 years.

Originally from Lutu in Wainimala, Naitasiri, Watisoni operates a carrier service along the route from Matanisau, Lutu, Waibasaga, Botenaulu, Nausori and into Suva before making the return trip home in the afternoon.

His passengers are mainly villagers from the highlands, many of whom travel to Suva to sell fresh produce at the market or attend to important business in the capital.

His day usually begins between midnight and 1am., a demanding routine that requires discipline, commitment and sacrifice.”It is not an easy job,” Watisoni says. “I thank God every day for his guidance and protection throughout my life and my work.”

For Watisoni, driving is more than simply transporting passengers from one destination to another.

It is a responsibility that carries the lives and livelihoods of the people who depend on him.

If his carrier is not full when he leaves the village, he stops along the route to pick up additional passengers, ensuring that no one is left behind if they need transport.

The journey itself is far from easy. The roads leading from the highlands are steep, winding and challenging, especially during the early hours of the morning when visibility is limited.

Every trip demands complete concentration. “The roads are difficult with many hills and slopes,” he explains. “When I am driving, I know I am responsible for many lives. My duty is to make sure everyone reaches their destination safely.

Behind every kilometre he travels is an even greater motivation his family.

Watisoni is married and the father of five children. Some are pursuing tertiary studies while others are completing high school.

Like many parents, he works tirelessly to ensure his children receive opportunities for a better education and a brighter future.

“It is our responsibility as fathers to provide for our families, everything I do is for my children.”

From Monday through Saturday, his passengers know they can rely on him.

On the rare occasion that illness prevents him from driving, he makes sure they are informed early so they can arrange alternative transport.

Building trust has been just as important as building his business. Despite rising fuel prices and increasing operating costs, Watisoni continues to persevere.

He admits that making ends meet has become more challenging, but he remains focused on working hard and serving his community.

As someone who has spent years overcoming challenges, Watisoni hopes young people will embrace opportunities instead of giving up when life becomes difficult.

“There are many opportunities out there,” he says. “You have to stay consistent, work hard and keep praying.

“There will always be obstacles, but with determination and faith, you can build a future for yourself and your family.”

For Watisoni Kaitaci, every journey begins in the darkness before dawn.

Yet through his dedication, faith and commitment to his passengers, he continues to brighten the lives of countless families who rely on him every single day.

item.title: DRUA WOMEN’S AWARD I Yee eyes bigger prize after Fan Player award
item.description: BEING named the 2026 Mogul Fan Player of the Year has only fuelled young McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women star Carletta Yee’s desire to achieve even greater success next season. The youngest member of the Drua squad, 18-year-old Carletta Yee received the fan-voted award at the club’s Annual Presentation Night held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Nadi on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
BEING named the 2026 Mogul Fan Player of the Year has only fuelled young McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women star Carletta Yee’s desire to achieve even greater success next season.

The youngest member of the Drua squad, 18-year-old Carletta Yee received the fan-voted award at the club’s Annual Presentation Night held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Nadi on Tuesday.

A fitting reward for a breakthrough campaign that saw her emerge as one of the side’s brightest performers.

While humbled by the recognition from supporters, Yee said the award was made even more special because of the environment created within the Drua family.

“It feels special. Being part of the Drua is so special and the environment we create here is something you always want to be a part of,” she said.

“Just getting to represent the Drua as a whole and being part of this amazing group of women and the coaches, I just feel so blessed. I’m looking forward to another great season with them next year.”

Rather than being satisfied with individual recognition, Yee has already set her sights on an even bigger target.

“I guess it just pushes me to win the Player of the Year next year,” she said.

The talented youngster admitted the pain of the Drua’s Super Rugby Women’s grand final defeat still lingers but believes it will become the team’s biggest source of motivation.

“I’m looking forward to another grand final next year. As our CEO said, we have to grab that feeling we felt after that loss and turn it into motivation to get the win next year. We’re just looking forward to everything next year brings and learning from this season and everything we’ve achieved so far.”

Yee dedicated the award to her family, especially her parents and sisters, thanking them for their unwavering support throughout her rugby journey.

“They’ve always been there for me since day one. Whether it’s home or away, they’re always in the stands supporting me.”

She also had a message for the loyal Drua supporters.

“We’re devastated that we couldn’t get the win, but I promise you all that next year we’re going to get another home grand final, and we’re going to win that grand final.”

Encouraging the next generation to embrace the sport, Yee urged young girls to give rugby a chance.

“Just try rugby. It’s for anyone. Any shape or size that you are, just try rugby. You never know what experience it gives you or what may come your way. It’s something you never want to miss out on.”

item.title: DRUA WOMEN’S AWARD I Drua Women hailed for inspiring a nation despite the loss
item.description: THE McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women may have fallen one step short of the Super Rugby Women’s title this season. Fijian Drua chief executive officer Jeff Miller believes the team’s greatest achievement extends far beyond the rugby field.
item.content:encoded:
THE McDonald’s Fiji Fijian Drua Women may have fallen one step short of the Super Rugby Women’s title this season.

Fijian Drua chief executive officer Jeff Miller believes the team’s greatest achievement extends far beyond the rugby field.

Speaking during the Drua Women’s Annual Presentation Night at the Sofitel Fiji Resort and Spa in Nadi on Tuesday night, Miller praised the players for delivering a season that had inspired a nation and transformed lives.

He reminded the audience that the club’s vision was built on three pillars – winning Super Rugby titles, inspiring a nation and changing lives for the better.

While the elusive championship slipped away in the home grand final against the NSW Waratahs, Miller said the team had achieved the other two goals in remarkable fashion.

“What you’ve achieved this year is nothing short of extraordinary,” he said.

“You’ve won a Super Rugby minor premiership, you’ve inspired a nation and you’ve changed lives for the better.”

Miller highlighted the historic achievement of Fiji hosting its first-ever Super Rugby Women’s grand final, describing it as a milestone for women’s rugby in Fiji. More than 4,000 spectators packed the venue, setting a new attendance record for a standalone women’s rugby match in Fiji.

He said everyone associated with the club should be proud of the landmark occasion.

“It showed that the team has captured the hearts of our people,” Miller said.

He added that young girls across Fiji now had role models they could identify with players from villages just like theirs who had proven it was possible to compete on rugby’s biggest stage.

“That is changing lives for the better,” he said. Miller thanked head coach Mike Legge and the coaching and management staff for guiding the team through another memorable campaign before paying tribute to the players.

“You truly are a special group,” he said.

“You’ve represented your families, your villages, your supporters and most importantly your country with humility, courage and pride.”

He said their dedication, belief in one another and relentless work ethic had inspired thousands of young girls to dream bigger, adding that this could become the team’s greatest legacy.

item.description: Protect your eyes | Why good vision, UV protection, and early treatment matter
